queue.recognise: You can recognise it by being a dawn redwood, a species known only from fossils until 1941, now 5.10 metres round, feathery and soft compared with the giant sequoia and other conifers standing nearby in the same former pinetum.
queue.story:
Until 1941 this species existed only as a fossil. Botanists had described Metasequoia from imprints in stone and assumed it had been gone for millions of years, and then a stand of them turned up alive in central China. Seed went out to the world's botanical gardens within a few years, and Baarn got some of it. This tree germinated around 1948, which makes it one of the first generation of dawn redwoods to grow in Europe since the species disappeared from the record entirely.

It has grown fast. It measured 4.22 metres around in 2008 and 5.10 metres by 2021, and over roughly the same decade its height went from 25.4 metres to 28.2. By the standards of its own kind it is still a child.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as one of the two giant cedars that flank the torii at the entrance to Noike Park, with a bamboo grove beside it.
queue.story:
Noike was a shrine to a water deity before it was anything else. In 1873 it became a public park under the government decree that created Japan's first parks, one of the earliest in the country, and in 2025 the national government named it a scenic site. Two springs from the volcanic Kuju plateau feed its pond, and they run at 12 to 13 degrees in every season.

The torii at the park entrance stands between two giant cedars. Japan's forest tree breeding centre lists the shrine's cedar at an estimated 800 years, 41 metres tall and 7.2 metres round, which no second source confirms, so take the age as an estimate.
